newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK rail firms dismiss report of cash woes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK rail firms dismiss report of cash woes.

text.p: Two British railway operators on Monday dismissed a pressure group study saying they were among four companies set to face heavy losses on their rail franchises.
Go-Ahead Group Plc and Prism Rail Plc both said the study, commissioned by pressure group Save Our Railways (SOR), was based on false assumptions.
The report said five out of the total 25 train operating companies, including Thameslink (owned by Go-Ahead) and three run by Prism, would make losses whatever assumptions were used.

Martin Ballinger, managing director of Go-Ahead, which owns the Thameslink line operating trains through London from the South Coast to Bedford, defended the revenue estimates on which his franchise bid was based.

"We stand by estimates that were prepared by our consultants," Ballinger told Reuters. "They estimate around five percent growth (in revenues) and that's more accurate for the railways we are concerned with."

The report hit shares in the companies, however. Shares in Go-Ahead ended the day 12-1/2p, or 2.5 percent, lower at 490p, while Prism stocks were 10p, or 2.8 percent, lower at 345p against a background of a generally firmer London market.
Giles Fearnley, chief executive of Prism said: "We are extremely angry that Save Our Railways have chosen to publish this report without any apparent attempt to consult with franchisees."

Prism said in a statement that although the report recognises the railways suffered through lack of investment prior to privatisation, it "takes no account of the revenue generating investment opportunities that are inherent in our own franchise plans."
SOR used four different assumptions, depending on likely increases in net revenue over the next seven years, as the basis for the study.
It forecast a further four operating companies would run into "very serious financial difficulties", though eight -- including Stagecoach Plc's South West Trains -- would make large profits.
"The overall summary suggests they have applied a 1-1/2 percent increase (in revenue) and said on that basis we will make a loss," Ballinger said.
"Unfortunately that doesn't take into account the fact that our Oxford (west of London) branch, which is called Thames Trains, has had enormous increases in revenue."
Prism said there was a whole range of factors which should contribute significantly to revenue growth, saying the report failed to reflect its "very substantial" investment in new trains.
"Given these factors, we have to view this report as a predominantly political document which has been released to coincide with the election campaign," Fearnley said.
